indicators.note: the letters are dressed up into a new arrangement

explanation.surface: A baker describes icing a cake with decorative strips.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a genuine baking picture: a Danish pastry often does have strips of icing across the top, so the definition and the fodder share a kitchen.
explanation.definitionFit: A Danish pastry is a sweet flaky bake, loosely called a cake.

indicators.note: tells you to go by how the word is spoken

blocks.note: cherished = DEAR, a word for someone held precious

explanation.surface: Someone declares their fondness for a cud-chewing animal.
explanation.walkthrough: DEAR and DEER are spelt differently but said the same way, so 'it's said' swaps one for the other.
explanation.definitionFit: Deer chew the cud, so they are ruminants.

indicators.note: the letters could possibly be rearranged into another word

explanation.surface: Something is approaching and may soon be within range, like a target.
explanation.walkthrough: Definition and fodder mean nearly the same thing, which makes the anagram easy to overlook: 'in range' reads as the second half of the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: something approaching its goal is getting close to it.

clue.text: Pay out to put page in post

indicators.note: says where: inside the other piece

blocks.note: to post a letter is to send it
p is the standard abbreviation for page

explanation.surface: Paying a postage fee in order to mail a page.
explanation.walkthrough: Post is the verb, as in posting a letter; the page abbreviation drops in after its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: laying out money is paying it out.

clue.text: Regarding mail sent to pals, sorted

indicators.note: the letters are sorted into a new order, as mail is at a depot

explanation.surface: Letters sent to friends are sorted at the post office.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole surface is about mail, so 'sorted' passes as a post-office word rather than an instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: An adjective for anything to do with the post office, as in an order or a vote sent by mail.

blocks.note: a hand tool for turning nuts, what Americans call a wrench
read as a noun: something that stretches across a gap

explanation.surface: Asking which tool you would need to build a bridge.
explanation.walkthrough: The second sense is a made-up noun, one who spans; the question mark and 'perhaps' own up to it. A spanner is British for a wrench.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses: a wrench-like hand tool, and literally a thing that spans a gap as a bridge does.

blocks.note: a verb for protesting bitterly, usually followed by 'against'
the steel bars a train runs along

explanation.surface: A commuter grumbling about the state of the railway lines.
explanation.walkthrough: To rail against something is to protest bitterly; here 'about' stands in for 'against'.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses: the steel bars a railway runs on, and a verb for protesting loudly.

indicators.note: the letters are bent out of shape into a new order

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 7 letters; the apostrophe is ignored

explanation.surface: A famous conductor leans over to have a quiet word with a player called Tom.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bent Tom's ear' is an idiom for talking at someone at length, which hides that 'bent' is the instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: Maestro is the respectful title for a distinguished conductor.

indicators.note: one piece holds the other inside it

blocks.note: Eve, the first woman in Genesis

explanation.surface: Someone dodges a president's wife who is carrying a placard.
explanation.walkthrough: 'First lady' suggests a president's wife; in crosswords it is usually Eve.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: dodging a question or a person is avoiding them.

indicators.note: the letters might perhaps form another word

explanation.surface: A steady electrical supply delivered through the mains.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sustained energy at mains' reads as electricity, which steers you away from human endurance.
explanation.definitionFit: Stamina is the ability to keep up effort over a long time.

clue.text: A mission digs out wrong conclusion

indicators.note: the letters are put out of order

explanation.surface: An expedition excavates and reaches a mistaken verdict.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads like an archaeological team digging its way to the wrong verdict; 'out' is the only instruction, and the wrong conclusion turns out to be a medical one.
explanation.definitionFit: A misdiagnosis is a wrong conclusion about what is causing an illness.

blocks.note: an ex is a former partner

explanation.surface: Ann, who used to work in newspapers, is now married or spoken for.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads 'attached' as being in a relationship; here it means joined on.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: land or a building taken over has been joined on to something larger.

blocks.note: a gate is a way in

explanation.surface: An official closes off the north-east gate.
explanation.walkthrough: Both pieces are everyday crossword fare: a compass point and a way in, simply set side by side.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to cancel out an argument or an effect.

clue.text: Heading off, cream too whipped in cafe

indicators.note: the first letter of the next word is removed
the letters are whipped up into a new order, as cream is

explanation.surface: A cafe order of cream that has been whipped.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Whipped' is a natural word for cream, so it is easy to miss that it scrambles the letters too.
explanation.definitionFit: A tea room is a small cafe serving tea and cakes.

clue.text: Rubber applied to paper, as erroneous

indicators.note: the answer lies on the words that follow, spread across them

explanation.surface: Using a rubber on paper to remove a mistake.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is exactly what the thing is for: rubbing out an error on paper.
explanation.definitionFit: A regional use: in Britain a rubber is the small block that rubs out pencil marks.

clue.text: Gag because the Parisian is inside

indicators.note: one piece sits within the other

explanation.surface: A comedian's joke about a Frenchman who stays indoors.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gag' looks like a joke; it is the verb, to stop someone speaking.
explanation.definitionFit: As verbs, gagging someone means stopping them speaking.

blocks.note: a bill is an account, abbreviated AC

explanation.surface: Someone named Bill will eventually concede the argument.
explanation.walkthrough: Bill looks like a man's name; it is an invoice.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, usually with 'to': consenting to a request or demand.

clue.text: Access to hospital, everyone gets to lobby

blocks.note: H is the abbreviation for hospital, added on

explanation.surface: Everyone arriving at a hospital must pass through its lobby.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Access to hospital' reads as one idea, but 'to' only means add the hospital abbreviation on; 'gets to' then joins the wordplay to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: An entrance hall is the lobby just inside a building's front door.

blocks.note: a verb: to burn something deliberately
a noun: a portable lamp, what Americans call a flashlight

explanation.surface: An instruction to ignite something.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads 'light' as a verb joining the phrase; it is the noun, a hand-held lamp.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses: a verb for burning something down, and a British word for a hand-held lamp.

clue.text: Smell you and I find in organic part of soil

blocks.note: hum is British slang for a bad smell

explanation.surface: Two gardeners notice a whiff coming from the compost.
explanation.walkthrough: HUM as a noun meaning a pong is British slang.
explanation.definitionFit: Humus is the dark decayed organic matter in soil.

clue.text: A drain at the earliest opportunity (inits)

blocks.note: to sap is to drain energy

explanation.surface: A plumber is asked to clear a drain as soon as possible.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drain' looks like a noun for plumbing; it is the verb, to sap. '(inits)' warns the answer is a set of initials.
explanation.definitionFit: ASAP stands for as soon as possible.

definitions.note: Lug means the whole ear; the answer is its lower part, a loose fit

blocks.note: OBE, Order of the British Empire, is an honour placed after a name

explanation.surface: Hauling a nobleman off to receive his title.
explanation.walkthrough: Lug looks like a verb, to drag; it is British slang for an ear. OBE is a British honour.
explanation.definitionFit: Lug is informal for the ear, and the lobe is its fleshy lower part.

explanation.surface: Asking whether there are menus for the gentlemen, American style.
explanation.walkthrough: Chaps is informal British for men, and US is the standard short form for American.
explanation.definitionFit: A menu is a list of options, on a computer screen or at a restaurant.

clue.text: Nimble cleaner restored my Chinese pew

indicators.note: the letters are rebuilt in a new order

explanation.surface: An agile cleaner has refurbished an old Chinese church bench.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nimble' belongs to the definition: a sweep had to climb and squeeze up flues.
explanation.definitionFit: A chimney sweep cleans soot from chimneys, a job needing agility.
